sections.h2: A roof that fits Agritopia's historic-style homes

That variety is part of the charm, and it also means there isn't one standard roof here.

Tile is confirmed on at least one Phase 4 home from 2005, and tile is common across the East Valley. Beyond that, materials follow the architecture. When a roof on a home like this needs work, the aim is to keep the profile, color and edge details true to the house so the repair or replacement doesn't stand out from the street.

Before we quote any job, we look at the existing material, the pitch and how the roof meets walls, porches and chimneys. That tells us whether a tile roof, an asphalt shingle roof or a low-slope section is the right way to match what's already there.

sections.h2: What two decades of Arizona sun does to a 2003 roof
sections.body:
Ground was broken for homes in Agritopia in 2003, so the earliest roofs are now roughly 18–23 years old. Concrete and clay tile can outlast that by a wide margin, but the felt underlayment under the tile usually doesn't. In our climate, felt often lasts about 20–25 years before it dries out, cracks and stops shedding water.

Tile hides this kind of wear. A roof can look fine from the sidewalk while the layer underneath is brittle at the eaves, in the valleys and around vents. Often the first clue is a ceiling stain after a monsoon storm.

If yours is one of the earlier builds, a roof inspection shows where the underlayment stands before a leak reaches the inside. Some homes here have already had new roofs, so if you bought recently, check your disclosure paperwork for the roof's history.
